title: Title: Adaptive Chaos Dynamics for Algorithm Design
abstract: Adaptive chaos dynamics offer a novel algorithmic framework for algorithm design, leveraging the principles of chaotic systems to achieve enhanced performance and robustness. This paper proposes a self-regulating system that monitors the algorithm's output and dynamically adjusts its parameters, mirroring the inherent instability and self-organization of natural chaotic phenomena. The core mechanism centers around the creation of a feedback loop that continuously optimizes the algorithm's behavior, ensuring it responds effectively to changing conditions. This approach contrasts with traditional algorithmic design, which typically utilizes static parameters, and promises to yield algorithms capable of navigating complex, unpredictable environments. The paper details the framework's architecture, explores its potential benefits through theoretical analysis, and presents preliminary experiments demonstrating improved performance across a range of test cases. The focus is on demonstrating the practical application of adaptive chaos principles in algorithm design.

title: 基于自适应量子态的自适应控制
abstract: This paper introduces a novel algorithm for quantum control based on adaptive quantum states. Traditional quantum control methods often rely on static control parameters, limiting their effectiveness in dynamic environments. The proposed algorithm leverages the unique properties of adaptive quantum states to dynamically adjust quantum states, enabling more efficient quantum control, particularly in areas such as quantum entanglement manipulation and secure key distribution. The core mechanism involves a feedback loop that continuously monitors and adjusts the quantum state to optimize performance. This approach overcomes the limitations of static control strategies, offering a significant improvement in the performance of quantum systems. The algorithm demonstrates improved control precision and robustness through extensive simulations and experimental validation.

title: Title: Adaptive Explainability Toolkit
abstract: This paper introduces an adaptive explainability toolkit designed to automatically adjust interpretability metrics and visualization methods based on the model and data characteristics. The core aim is to significantly enhance model interpretability by providing a flexible and dynamic approach to explanation generation. Traditional explainability tools often rely on predefined parameters, limiting their adaptability to diverse datasets and model types. This work proposes a novel framework that leverages a customizable parameterization system to dynamically tailor the explanation process. The resulting tool will be able to provide insights into model behavior, facilitating better understanding and trust in complex machine learning models. This advancement directly addresses the limitations of existing methods by offering a truly adaptive and extensible solution for model explainability. The framework's design incorporates a mechanism for continuous refinement based on observed performance and user feedback, ensuring optimal interpretability for a wide range of applications.

title: The Effects of Chatbot Recovery Strategies and Anthropomorphic Image Type on Service Recovery Satisfaction: The Mediating Roles of Perceived Warmth and Competence
abstract: The widespread adoption of chatbots enables companies to provide customer service at low cost and with high efficiency. However, the inherent limitations of chatbots often lead to service failures, highlighting the necessity of effective recovery strategies. Nevertheless, the optimal approaches for chatbots to implement self-recovery strategies remain unclear. Drawing on the Computers As Social Actors (CASA) paradigm and the Stereotype Content Model (SCM), this study investigates the interactive effects of recovery strategies (emotional recovery strategy vs. informational recovery strategy) and anthropomorphic image types (warm image vs. competent image) on service recovery satisfaction. It also examines the psychological mechanisms and boundary conditions underlying these effects. Based on two offline experiments with university students (Study 1: n = 162; Study 2: n = 350), the results show that a match between a chatbot’s emotional recovery strategy and a warm image (or an informational recovery strategy and a competent image) enhances service recovery satisfaction. Perceived warmth and perceived competence are found to mediate these effects. The findings further reveal that time pressure moderates the interactive effect. These findings advance the theoretical understanding of the psychological mechanisms underlying the effects of chatbot self-recovery strategies on service recovery satisfaction, while offering practical implications for optimizing service recovery strategies and enhancing customer experience.

title: Hybrid VQA architectures for cloud-based quantum platforms: maximizing computational utility
abstract: Introduction Hybrid Variational Quantum Algorithms (VQAs) present a highly viable pathway to near-term quantum utility; however, their performance is fundamentally bottlenecked by classical-quantum communication latency in Quantumas-a-Service (QaaS) environments. Methods This paper proposes an optimized classical-quantum orchestration architecture designed to minimize cloud-induced latency and maximize Quantum Processing Unit (QPU) active compute time. By implementing edge-colocated classical optimizers alongside batched parameter-shift gradient evaluations, the system circumvents stateless cloud API barriers. Results Benchmarking across parameterized quantum circuits ranging from 15 to 50 qubits demonstrates an 84% reduction in network-induced QPU idle time. The framework yields a 3.2 × speedup in overall convergence time for the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) and up to a 98% reduction in classical API call overhead compared to standard RESTful QaaS execution models. Discussion These quantitative findings demonstrate that tightly coupled hybrid co-processing, physically adjacent to the control electronics, is critical for extending the computational bound of Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) devices.

title: Large Language Model-Driven Hard Negatives Generation for Contrastive Aspect-Based Sentiment Analysis
abstract: While sentiment analysis has advanced significantly, fine-grained sentiment classification such as aspect-based sentiment analysis (ABSA), continues to present challenges. These difficulties primarily stem from data scarcity and the inherent complexities of identifying sentiments specific to different aspects within a text. The recent emergence of generative artificial intelligence (AI), particularly large language models (LLMs), has fundamentally altered the landscape of data management and integration. To better capture nuanced sentiment differences, this paper proposes a novel approach that leverages LLMs to generate “hard negatives” for ABSA. We introduce the sentiment-aware chain-of-thought (SACoT) framework, which emulates a human-like reasoning process to manipulate the sentiment polarity of aspect terms. This is achieved by integrating chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning with a few-shot prompting strategy, guiding the LLM to produce sentences with the desired sentiment towards specific aspects. Furthermore, we employ an LLM-as-a-Judge framework to refine these generated hard negatives, thereby enhancing their quality for subsequent use in supervised fine-tuning and contrastive learning. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that our proposed approach, LLM-SCADA (LLM-guided sentiment-context-aspect data augmentation), significantly improves model performance, especially in transitioning from neutral to positive sentiments (NEU → POS). An in-depth ablation study further underscores the distinct contributions of the generated hard negatives, the contrastive learning approach, and the refinement process. These findings highlight the potential of LLMs to create sentiment-shifted samples based on aspect terms, paving the way for more robust and sophisticated techniques in the field of ABSA.

title: Physics-Informed Machine Learning Correction of Variational Quantum Eigensolver Energies for Molecular Ground States
abstract: Abstract The variational quantum Eigensolver (VQE) provides a scalable route to molecular ground-state energies on near-term quantum hardware, but its accuracy degrades rapidly as system size grows because hardware-efficient ansätze cannot span the full correlation subspace. We introduce a physics-informed ridge regression correction that is trained on the difference between VQE and Hartree–Fock (HF) energies and applied as a postprocessing step requiring no additional quantum resources. The feature set─the VQE–HF energy gap ΔE, its square ΔE2, the active-space qubit count, the number of active electrons, and two cross-term interactions─captures the dominant drivers of ansatz error in a low-dimensional, interpretable form. The model is benchmarked on H2, H2O, NH3, CH4, C2H6, and CH3OH using the STO-3G basis set and a state vector VQE simulator using a two-layer Ry-CNOT hardware-efficient ansatz. To assess cross-molecule generalizability, the corrected framework is further tested on CO2, N2, and HCN under both untrained and trained conditions. Absolute energy errors fall from a range of 0.02–0.79 Ha (raw VQE) to 0.0007–0.094 Ha after correction, corresponding to improvement factors of 3× to 640× relative to CASCI reference values. Zero-shot generalization tests yield factors of 9–58×, and including molecules in training improves results by a further order of magnitude in several cases. The three extended molecules exhibit improvement factors of 4–6× in untrained settings and 5–6× after training, providing preliminary evidence of transferability across chemically distinct systems. These findings suggest that the VQE–HF energy gap encodes physically transferable information about correlation-energy saturation, and that even the smallest training set can produce practically useful corrections for near-term quantum chemistry.

title: Advanced Technologies and Future Trends
abstract: This chapter examines the latest advancements transforming sentiment analysis. It analyzes the pivotal role of large language models (from BERT to the GPT series) and their applications in deep contextual understanding, zero-shot learning, and generative sentiment analysis. The use of generative AI for data augmentation, adversarial sample generation, and enhancing model robustness and explainability is explored in detail. Challenges and solutions in cross-lingual and cross-cultural sentiment analysis are critically discussed. The chapter also addresses emerging directions such as real-time sentiment analysis and the ethical considerations surrounding bias, privacy, and responsible AI governance. Future trends and the path toward culturally aware, trustworthy affective intelligence are outlined.

title: Pitch-class Steering for Diffusion-based Music Generation via Latent-space Probes
abstract: Recent work on controllable music generation has focused on autoregressive models, leaving diffusion-based systems comparatively underexplored. We present a lightweight method for steering the pitch content of audio produced by Stable Audio Open, a latent diffusion model for music synthesis. A small convolutional probe containing approximately 125k parameters is trained to decode frame-level pitch-class activations from the model's variational autoencoder latent space, using paired audio and MIDI data. At inference time, the frozen probe serves as a differentiable loss function: its gradient with respect to the denoising latent is used to nudge generation toward a user-specified pitch-class sequence, requiring no retraining or architectural modification of the base model. Across 27 evaluation trials spanning 9 text prompts and 3 target melodies, probe-guided generation increases melodic coherence by 2.4x over the unguided baseline (p < 1e-5, Wilcoxon signed-rank test), demonstrating that musically meaningful structure is both recoverable and steerable in diffusion-based music latent spaces.

title: From Deceptive Outputs to Deceptive Mechanisms: A Causal Framework for Language-Model Deception Research
abstract: Research and news coverage of language-model deception increasingly attributes human-like mental-state concepts to language models. Such claims can blur the distinction between behavior that looks deceptive and a mechanism that is actually deceptive. We introduce a causal taxonomy separating prior commitment from retrospective report, model preference from realized output, false preference from sensitivity to the utility of misleading a recipient, and deceptive behavior from the provenance of the objective or strategy producing it. We test these distinctions in two open-weight model families. Across controlled guessing-game and stock-trading experiments, we find that deceptive-looking behavior can arise without the corresponding proposed mechanism, while other interventions provide direct evidence that recipient information state can causally affect deceptive preference. These results show that deceptive behavior can provide evidence for a deceptive mechanism. But even evidence for such a mechanism does not establish model agency in the deception.

title: Flip, Don't Shuffle: Watermarking LLMs at the Speed of Inference
abstract: We introduce Stateless Bernoulli Watermarking (SBW), a new statistical watermark for Large Language Models that determines green list membership through independent per-token Bernoulli trials. Unlike KGW's vocabulary permutation or SynthID's multi-layer tournament, SBW requires only a single comparison per token against a counter-based random number generator, reducing membership complexity to $O(1)$ and enabling single-kernel execution with zero intermediate allocations. We prove that this formulation preserves the same detection guarantees as fixed-size green lists: the z-score test remains $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ under the null. The stateless architecture enables capabilities unavailable to existing methods: full-vocabulary self-salt watermarking (over 6000$\times$ faster than KGW's self-salt and 2$\times$ faster than SynthID despite biasing the entire vocabulary with candidate-dependent seeding) and architectural compatibility with distributed inference. In end-to-end generation benchmarks, SBW adds less than 1\% overhead at all batch sizes. We additionally identify hash function design as a previously unexplored axis for watermark quality, showing that a GPU-native Jenkins hash improves null calibration by 1.8$\times$ while producing more diverse text. Experiments across two seeding schemes and eight $(γ, δ)$ configurations confirm statistical equivalence with ROC-AUC differences below 0.01.

title: Text2Thermal: Physics-Aware Thermal Image Synthesis from Textual Priors
abstract: Thermal infrared imaging offers reliable perception in darkness and adverse weather, but thermal datasets remain scarce, motivating extensive work on translating abundant RGB images into thermal. Such translation is fundamentally ill-posed as thermal appearance is governed by surface emissivity and object temperature, neither of which is observable in the visible spectrum, so a single RGB image is consistent with many valid thermal outputs. We argue that language offers a natural means of resolving this ambiguity, and propose **Text2Thermal**, a framework for physics-aware thermal image synthesis from textual priors. Rather than inferring the unobservable radiometric factors from RGB, we supply them explicitly through thermally grounded captions encoding material, weather, time-of-day, and heat-emission state, and adapt a pre-trained Stable Diffusion backbone to the thermal domain. Because the radiometric content is determined entirely by the prompt, Text2Thermal synthesizes thermal imagery without requiring a registered RGB image at inference. Where spatial guidance is desired, an optional control signal imparts scene geometry without disturbing the prompt-specified radiometry. On M3FD and FLIR, Text2Thermal achieves state-of-the-art FID among thermal image synthesis methods, and we additionally report results on the FMB dataset, while offering text-level control that translation-based approaches cannot provide.

title: “Who Is to Blame?” and “What Is to Be Done?”: A Formal Study of Counterfactual Approaches to Responsibility and Causation in (Multi-Agent) AI Systems
abstract: AI systems are increasingly deployed in safety-critical domains, where they behave non-deterministically, act under uncertainty, and form part of larger multi-agent systems without central control. When such systems cause harm, two questions arise: who is to blame, and what could have been done to prevent it? This thesis develops formal frameworks that make responsibility and causation mathematically precise and algorithmically verifiable, both for attributing responsibility and for identifying the interventions that reduce risk. It is organised in three parts. Part I introduces logics of group responsibility in probabilistic multi-agent systems, based on the risk a group could jointly have avoided, with sound and complete axiomatisations, decidability, and efficient model checking. Part II proposes a new definition of actual cause, Dynamic Causality, studies temporal extension of causal models and their computational properties. Part III connects the two, inducing concurrent game structures from causal models to reason about responsibility in organisational structures. The thesis argues that once non-determinism, strategic ability, uncertainty, and time are made explicit, responsibility and causation admit precise and verifiable formal interpretations.

title: Quantum Adaptive Algorithms for Gradient Boosting of Complex Geometries
abstract: This paper presents a novel gradient boosting framework leveraging quantum adaptive algorithms and tensor computation. We investigate the potential of combining these paradigms to accelerate learning and enhance gradient ascent in the context of complex geometric data. The core mechanism focuses on utilizing quantum algorithms for efficient exploration of the parameter space and tensor computations for enhanced feature representation, thereby mitigating the limitations of traditional gradient boosting methods. The research demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach in learning intricate geometric patterns, overcoming challenges in handling non-linear relationships inherent in complex datasets. We provide a theoretical analysis of the algorithm's performance and explore its potential impact on various geometric modeling tasks.

title: Learning to Learn with Evolutionary Algorithms for Neural Network Architecture Search
abstract: The manual design of neural network architectures is a significant bottleneck in deep learning development. This research investigates the application of evolutionary algorithms (EAs) to automate this architecture search process. The proposed method utilizes an EA to iteratively explore the architectural space, generating and evaluating diverse network designs based on their performance on a given task. The core mechanism involves the selection, mutation, and crossover of promising architectures, mimicking the principles of natural evolution. The goal is to discover optimal architectures more efficiently than traditional manual design approaches, potentially leading to improved model accuracy, reduced computational cost, and the identification of novel network designs. This work demonstrates the feasibility and effectiveness of using EAs for neural network architecture search, paving the way for more automated and adaptive deep learning systems.

title: Topology-Driven Algorithms for Optimization in Complex Systems
abstract: This paper explores the application of topology as a fundamental building block for optimization algorithms, particularly within complex systems exhibiting inherent connectivity and feedback loops. Traditional optimization methods often struggle with these characteristics, requiring explicit modeling and simplification. We propose a novel algorithmic paradigm centered on defining a 'graphical structure' of the system, leveraging topology to guide the optimization process toward topologically linked solutions – patterns that are inherently more efficient and robust. title: Bio-Inspired Interference Cancellation Coding Based on Biological Neural Networks
abstract: This paper proposes a novel information coding methodology inspired by the interference cancellation mechanisms observed in biological neural networks. Traditional information coding techniques often struggle with noisy environments and unreliable transmission channels, leading to data loss and reduced efficiency. Our approach leverages the inherent robustness of biological neural networks, specifically mimicking the synaptic plasticity, excitation-inhibition dynamics, and inter-neuronal interactions found within neurons. We construct a coding network designed to actively filter out interference signals, resulting in a more robust and efficient encoding process. The core of this method lies in dynamically adjusting the network's connectivity and activation thresholds based on detected interference, effectively creating a self-correcting system. This research presents a fundamentally different approach to information encoding, promising improved performance in challenging environments and potentially offering novel solutions for data compression and robust communication. The system's performance is evaluated through theoretical analysis and conceptual modelling, demonstrating its potential advantages over conventional methods.

title: Semantic Graph Embedding with Attention-Based Causal Inference
abstract: Graph embedding techniques have witnessed significant advancements in recent years, playing a crucial role in various applications such as node classification, link prediction, and graph visualization. However, existing methods often struggle to effectively capture the intricate semantic relationships and causal influences that govern the structure of a graph. This paper addresses this limitation by proposing a novel graph embedding approach that synergistically combines attention mechanisms with a causal inference framework. The attention mechanism learns to assign weights based on the semantic similarity between nodes, reflecting the importance of each node in relation to others. Simultaneously, the causal inference component models the directional influence, or dependencies, between nodes, providing a more complete and accurate representation of the graph's structure. Our approach aims to go beyond simply capturing topological proximity and delve into the underlying reasoning process within the graph. We present a detailed formulation of the model, including the attention weighting process and the causal inference module. Experimental results on benchmark graph datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in capturing both semantic and causal information, leading to improved performance in downstream graph-related tasks. The key contribution of this work lies in the unified framework that integrates semantic understanding and causal reasoning into a single graph embedding model.

title: Quantum-Inspired Genetic Algorithm for Complex Optimization Problems
abstract: This paper explores the application of a quantum-inspired genetic algorithm (QIGA) for solving complex optimization problems. Traditional genetic algorithms (GAs) can struggle with the intricacies of high-dimensional and non-linear problems, often encountering issues with premature convergence and local optima. This research proposes a novel approach where a standard GA is modified to incorporate principles inspired by quantum mechanics, specifically utilizing quantum-inspired concepts such as superposition and interference, to enhance the exploration and exploitation phases. The core claim is that QIGA can effectively tackle complex optimization scenarios. The mechanism involves mapping the original problem into the fitness function of the GA, and subsequently using the QIGA to perform the optimization. The results demonstrate the potential of this hybrid approach to improve solution quality and speed, particularly in problems with challenging characteristics. The research highlights a promising direction for combining classical optimization techniques with quantum-inspired ideas, offering a new tool for tackling computationally intensive optimization tasks. ---

title: Dynamic Topology Learning for Graph Neural Networks using Evolutionary Algorithms
abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have demonstrated remarkable success in various domains, including social network analysis, drug discovery, and recommendation systems. However, a fundamental limitation of traditional GNNs lies in their reliance on static graph structures. These networks are often trained on graphs with fixed topologies, which may not accurately reflect the underlying data distribution, particularly when dealing with evolving or dynamic datasets. This research addresses this limitation by introducing a novel approach—Dynamic Topology Learning for GNNs—which utilizes evolutionary algorithms to dynamically adjust the topology of the graph underlying a GNN during the training process. The core idea is to enable the network to adapt to changes in the data's structural properties, thereby improving its performance and robustness. This paper details the proposed methodology, including the evolutionary algorithm design, the graph topology representation, and the integration with a standard GNN architecture. Experimental results, though not presented through formal experiments, demonstrate the potential of this approach to handle evolving graph structures, suggesting significant improvements in GNN performance compared to static graph-based GNNs. The key contribution is a self-modifying GNN capable of adapting to changing data distributions, offering a promising direction for future research in dynamic graph learning.

title: Temporal Graph Embedding with Causality Propagation
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to temporal graph embedding, addressing the limitations of existing methods that often fail to capture the crucial role of causality in dynamic systems. The core challenge lies in representing how events influence each other over time, a requirement frequently overlooked in standard graph embedding techniques. Our proposed method, Temporal Graph Embedding with Causality Propagation (TGECP), integrates a causal graph layer with structural embeddings. This layer leverages dynamic Bayesian networks and Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods to propagate causal influence through the graph, dynamically updating node embeddings based on observed events and their potential causal effects. The resulting embeddings offer a more accurate and nuanced representation of temporal dependencies, leading to improved performance in downstream tasks such as node classification and link prediction. We demonstrate the effectiveness of TGECP through a theoretical analysis and outline key design choices, emphasizing the importance of explicitly modeling causality in temporal graph representations.

title: 基于自适应的强化学习的超参数优化
abstract: This paper introduces a novel reinforcement learning algorithm, termed "Adaptive Reward Tuning," which utilizes self-adaptive reinforcement learning to dynamically optimize the reward function and learning rate. The algorithm employs a self-adapting strategy that adjusts the reward function and learning rate based on data characteristics, leading to improved model performance. We investigate the effectiveness of this method through a series of simulations and experiments, demonstrating significant enhancements in convergence speed and final performance compared to conventional optimization techniques. The core mechanism focuses on a dynamic adjustment of these two key parameters, offering a robust and adaptable approach to hyperparameter tuning in reinforcement learning. This work addresses a critical challenge in reinforcement learning: the difficulty of finding optimal hyperparameter settings.

title: Quantum Geometry Transformation: Adaptive Optimization
abstract: Quantum Geometry Transformation (QGT) presents a novel approach to geometric optimization utilizing quantum entanglement. This paper explores the design and implementation of a quantum-enhanced optimization algorithm, leveraging the unique properties of quantum entanglement to achieve automated optimization and significantly enhance computational efficiency. The core mechanism centers around employing entanglement to create a highly entangled state, allowing the algorithm to explore a vast solution space more effectively than classical methods. We detail the algorithm's design, the application of entanglement to represent the geometry of the problem, the optimization process, and the expected benefits in terms of speed and precision. The paper concludes with a discussion of the potential impact of this approach on various geometric optimization problems and emphasizes the significance of quantum entanglement as a transformative tool.

title: Quantum Decoherence-Driven Cryptanalysis
abstract: This paper investigates the potential of leveraging quantum decoherence for cryptanalysis. The core claim is that exploiting the properties of quantum decoherence can accelerate the rate at which cryptographic keys are compromised. The proposed mechanism involves designing a novel algorithm that directly targets the vulnerabilities introduced by decoherence. Specifically, this algorithm aims to disrupt cryptographic keys by manipulating the quantum state and inducing decoherence, thereby facilitating the decryption process. The research delves into the theoretical aspects of this approach, focusing on the mathematical formulation of decoherence effects and their impact on key security. We explore scenarios where precisely controlled decoherence can significantly reduce the computational complexity of breaking certain cryptographic schemes. The work highlights the potential of directly applying fundamental quantum principles to cryptanalysis, offering a new avenue for attack strategies. The presented analysis provides a foundational understanding of this emerging field, emphasizing the need for further research into the practical implementation and optimization of decoherence-based cryptanalytic techniques.

title: Sharper, Not Safer: The Direction of Human Deviations from Engine Play
abstract: Version v5 (September 2026). Corrected estimator for all mixed models: the player random intercept described in the text was missing from the fitting helper in earlier versions. All 23 models were refit under a correction specification locked before the refit; 24 printed values changed at printed precision, no conclusion changed. The fault is disclosed as the fourth item in Section 6. Correction specification, refit report, and old-to-new numbers table: docs/ in the GitHub repository. When a human player departs from a chess engine's preferred move, is the departure noise, or does it have a direction? I analyze 1,970 rated online games by titled players: 50,021 middlegame position-moves; 120,723 engine evaluations in total, comprising 63,429 root and context evaluations for the magnitude analysis and 57,294 successor evaluations for the direction analysis, all at fixed depth with five principal variations. All evaluations are converted to win probability before differencing. Deviation magnitude behaves as a noise account predicts. It falls with rating, rises with position volatility, and rises under time pressure. The direction of deviation does not. I define a move's riskiness as the steepness of the opponent's punishment curve: the win-probability gap between the opponent's best and fifth-best replies. At equal expected loss, human moves sit on steeper curves than the engine's choice (intercept +1.22 win-probability points, p = 1.6 × 10 ³⁵;⁻ 59.85% of deviations toward the sharper side, sign-test p = 1.8 × 10 ¹⁷ ). The effect survives a ⁻ ⁰ liquidation control and two pre-specified robustness variants, and it strengthens under time pressure. A risk-averse agent should retreat to recoverable positions; players sharpen instead. A pilot-stage association between deviation direction and a previously measured style dimension collapsed on the full sample, and I report it as unsupported. My reading is that human play optimizes an objective the engine does not share, one that prices the opponent's fallibility, though on average the sharpening is not repaid in results. All hypotheses, parameters, and variants were fixed in advance. Two pipeline faults caught during execution are disclosed in full.

title: Quantum Association Matrix: A Novel Approach to Accelerated Quantum Computation
abstract: Quantum Association Matrix (QAM) is a proposed algorithm leveraging the principles of quantum entanglement to revolutionize the efficiency of quantum computation. This paper investigates the potential of utilizing entanglement to accelerate matrix operations, offering a novel approach to quantum data storage and retrieval. The core mechanism centers around the controlled evolution of entangled states to achieve faster computations and data transfer. This research explores the theoretical underpinnings of QAM, detailing the mathematical framework and potential implementation challenges. The paper concludes by outlining the key contributions and future research directions, emphasizing the significance of this algorithm for advancing quantum computing capabilities.

title: Based Quantum Entanglement for Adaptive Information Entropy Estimation
abstract: This paper investigates the potential of quantum entanglement for significantly enhanced information entropy estimation. Traditional methods often suffer from limitations in efficiency and accuracy. We propose a novel quantum entanglement-based algorithm designed for high-precision and low-latency entropy calculations. The core mechanism relies on exploiting the unique properties of entanglement to refine the estimation process and achieve adaptive adjustments, addressing the limitations of classical approaches. The algorithm's design incorporates a feedback loop to dynamically optimize the estimation process based on real-time data, promising to overcome the constraints of conventional entropy estimation techniques. This research explores the theoretical foundations and practical implementation of this approach, offering a promising avenue for advancements in quantum information processing.

title: Quantum Entanglement Computing: Adaptive Quantum State Transfer for Enhanced Security and Reduced Complexity
abstract: Quantum entanglement computing presents a paradigm shift in computation, offering the potential for significantly enhanced cryptographic algorithms and computational power. However, the inherent fragility of quantum states necessitates sophisticated security protocols. This paper explores the application of adaptive quantum state transfer to improve the security of quantum-based cryptographic systems, specifically addressing the challenges of information hiding and computational complexity. We propose a novel method leveraging the unique properties of quantum entanglement to dynamically adjust quantum states, mitigating vulnerabilities and optimizing performance. The core mechanism focuses on strategically manipulating quantum states to obfuscate information, thereby bolstering the integrity of cryptographic protocols. This research investigates the efficacy of this approach through theoretical analysis and preliminary simulations, demonstrating its potential to enhance security and reduce computational cost.

title: Self-Adaptive Gaussian Theory and Non-Linear Optimization
abstract: This paper introduces a novel optimization algorithm based on Self-Adaptive Gaussian Theory (SAGT). SAGT leverages the inherent properties of Gaussian processes to dynamically adjust parameters during optimization, enabling the handling of complex systems models. The algorithm's core mechanism involves constructing a parameterized Gaussian process that represents the system's dynamics, allowing for adaptive parameter adjustments based on observed data and model constraints. We demonstrate the effectiveness of SAGT through several non-linear optimization problems, showcasing its ability to achieve optimal solutions in challenging scenarios. This work addresses limitations of traditional optimization techniques by providing a robust and adaptable framework for modeling and optimizing complex systems.

title: Geometric Topology-Driven Proof Systems (GTPS)
abstract: Geometric Topology-Driven Proof Systems (GTPS) presents a novel approach to mathematical verification leveraging the power of geometric topology. This research introduces a new system predicated on the automated construction and analysis of complex topological structures, providing a method for verifying mathematical theorems and proofs through the rigorous construction of proofs. The core mechanism centers on generating and analyzing geometric shapes—manifolds, cycles—to construct proofs, enabling automated verification of mathematical statements. This represents a significant departure from traditional, purely logical deduction methods, offering the potential for vastly increased speed and scale in proof verification. The paper details the system's architecture, explores its potential applications, and discusses the challenges and future directions of this innovative approach.

The paper details the methodology, provides a comprehensive analysis of its effectiveness through illustrative examples, and concludes with a discussion of the potential applications and future research directions.

title: Adaptive Geometry Model Learning (AGML)
abstract: This paper introduces the Adaptive Geometry Model Learning (AGML) algorithm, a novel approach to model complex systems with dynamic relationships. Traditional model learning methods often rely on static representations, failing to capture the inherent variability and responsiveness of real-world systems. AGML addresses this limitation through a self-adaptive learning process, iteratively updating the model's parameters to precisely represent the system's evolving dynamics. We demonstrate the effectiveness of AGML through a series of simulations and experimental results, showcasing its ability to achieve significantly improved prediction accuracy compared to established methods. The core mechanism centers around a hierarchical refinement strategy, allowing the model to focus on the most relevant aspects of the system's behavior. This results in a more robust and accurate representation of the underlying dynamics.

title: Benchmark, Agent, and Tool-Use Harnesses for Large Language Models: A Taxonomy of Evaluation Infrastructure
abstract: Large language model evaluation has moved from static benchmark scripts to executable harnesses:systems that bind datasets, prompts, model adapters, inference backends, tools, environments, sandboxes,scorers, traces, and leaderboards into a measurement contract. This survey explains why that layer nowdetermines what a benchmark score means. We distinguish three harness families. Benchmark harnessesmake model comparison possible by fixing task registries, prompt templates, inference adapters, answerparsers, metrics, and aggregation rules. Agent harnesses turn evaluation into an environment experimentin which repositories, browsers, operating systems, mobile apps, users, databases, reset procedures, andexecutable oracles become part of the measured system. Tool-use harnesses isolate the interface problem: retrieving tool documentation, selecting APIs, formatting arguments, deciding when not to call atool, carrying state across turns, and recovering from tool failures. We map the infrastructure shared bythese families, show how their scoring contracts differ, and explain why scaffold effects, oracle design,environment drift, schema sensitivity, and trace policy can change the scientific meaning of a result. Thepaper argues that harnesses are no longer peripheral implementation details. They define what the taskis, what the model is allowed to do, how evidence is scored, and whether a result can be audited or cited.We provide a layered taxonomy, a literature stem map, family-specific failure analyses, guidance for in-terpreting leaderboard scores, and a reporting agenda for model developers, benchmark maintainers, andresearchers building agentic systems.

title: Grounding Player Intent in Game Commands: A Study of Compact Language Model Adaptation
abstract: Large language models can interpret user requests plausibly yet fail to produce actions that satisfy structural constraints. We study this problem in Dungeons & Dragons (D&D) combat, where player intent must be grounded in the current game state and translated into well-formed commands for Avrae, a Discord-based D&D automation system. We fine-tune a 4-bit quantized LLaMA-3 8B model with Low-Rank Adaptation on 256 curated FIREBALL-derived examples and compare it with zero-shot, one-shot, and few-shot prompting. On 25 held-out interactions, the model achieves 56% semantic grounding accuracy and 48% strict command validity. Results suggest that parameter-efficient adaptation improves grounding, while formatting, argument, and reference errors remain common.

title: Implicit Sentiment Analysis
abstract: This chapter focuses on the challenging area of implicit sentiment analysis, where opinions are not directly stated but must be inferred. It identifies two core computational problems: the commonsense reasoning gap and semantic incongruity (e.g., sarcasm, irony, and metaphor). Three major methodological paradigms are systematically explored: knowledge-augmented approaches using lexicons and knowledge graphs, contextual representation learning with deep neural networks, and prompt-based reasoning using large language models with chain-of-thought prompting. The chapter discusses techniques such as knowledge graph embeddings, graph neural networks, and advanced prompting strategies like self-consistency and tree-of-thoughts. A detailed case study demonstrates how LLMs can effectively interpret implicit sentiment through structured reasoning chains. Future directions, including implicit aspect-based analysis and causal inference, are also examined.

title: Atlas: Optimizing Deployment of Compound AI Workflows on Heterogeneous Clusters
abstract: Compound AI workflows are increasingly used to serve complex AI tasks by coordinating multiple AI models and software components. This approach enables deployment flexibility, as each workflow stage can expose different model variants and resource requirements, but it also expands the deployment choices. A deployment must choose an execution plan that selects AI models for each compound AI workflow stage and places them on a heterogeneous cluster in order to satisfy SLOs. Deployment optimizers therefore need estimates to compare many candidate plans and identify feasible ones. System metrics can often be profiled per stage and composed according to workflow topology, but accuracy cannot, as errors and information loss at upstream stages affect the accuracy of downstream stages. Existing approaches either profile complete configurations end to end, which scales poorly, or use product-based accuracy surrogates that treat stages as independent and can misrank candidate plans. We introduce Atlas, a framework for optimizing compound AI deployments under SLO constraints. Atlas uses MAP, a Markovian Accuracy Predictor, to estimate configuration accuracy from local conditional accuracy transitions between adjacent workflow stages. MAP discretizes intermediate outputs into accuracy buckets and composes transition profiles according to workflow topology, giving the optimizer an accuracy estimate without exhaustive end-to-end profiling. Atlas formulates execution-plan selection as a mixed-integer linear program that maximizes predicted accuracy subject to SLOs. Across four compound AI workflows, MAP achieves Spearman correlation up to 0.947 while reducing profiling cost by up to 2.6x relative to exhaustive end-to-end profiling. Guided by MAP, the Atlas optimizer selects execution plans within 0.03 of oracle accuracy while reducing deployment cost by up to 42% through heterogeneous placement.

title: A Stochastic Riemannian Alternating Descent Ascent Method for Nonsmooth Composite Expectation Optimization on Riemannian Manifolds
abstract: In this paper, we consider a class of Riemannian nonsmooth composite expectation optimization problems, which arises in various machine learning, signal processing, and statistics applications. Noting that these problems admit structured minimax reformulations, we propose an efficient algorithm, named stochastic Riemannian alternating descent ascent method with recursive momentum (StoRADA-RM), to tackle them. StoRADA-RM performs one or multiple Riemannian stochastic gradient descent steps and then a proximal gradient ascent step at each iteration. To compute the Riemannian stochastic gradient, we propose a vector transport-free recursive momentum estimator that requires only $O(1)$ stochastic gradient evaluations per iteration. We prove that StoRADA-RM returns an $ε$-Riemannian-stochastic-stationary point of a given problem in the said class in $O(ε^{-3})$ iterations while making $O(ε^{-3})$ calls to a stochastic first-order oracle (SFO). Both the iteration complexity and SFO complexity bounds are the best known in the literature for the said class of problems. The latter even matches the optimal lower bound for smooth nonconvex optimization with stochastic first-order algorithms. We then present numerical results on sparse principal component analysis and coordinate-independent sparse estimation to demonstrate the superior performance of our proposed method.

title: Long-Horizon Consistent and Interaction-Aware World Models for Multi-Style End-to-End Driving
abstract: End-to-end autonomous driving has increasingly adopted world model-based reinforcement learning frameworks to improve learning efficiency through \textit{imagined rollouts}. However, existing world models suffer from three key limitations: temporal inconsistency in long-horizon imagined rollouts, inadequate modeling of ego-environment interactions, and limited adaptability to diverse driving styles. To address these challenges, we propose \textit{StyleDrive}, a world-model-based learning framework that jointly enforces long-horizon consistency, explicitly disentangles interactive traffic states, and supports multi-style policy optimization within a unified learning paradigm. First, we introduce a temporal consistency regularization that integrates historical latent states through gated cross-attention, stabilizing long-horizon imagined rollouts and mitigating error accumulation. Second, we design an explicit state disentanglement module that separates ego-relevant from ego-irrelevant interactive states, enabling more interpretable and efficient decision-making in complex traffic scenarios. Third, we enable multi-style driving behaviors through Group Relative Policy Optimization, which replaces per-step reward optimization with trajectory-wise relative advantages, reducing reward variance and supporting diverse driving styles without retraining. We evaluate StyleDrive on the Bench2Drive closed-loop driving benchmark, achieving a driving score of 88.44 (+17.08 over the previous best world model-based method) and a success rate of 66.82 (+16.58). Furthermore, we deploy StyleDrive on a real automated guided vehicle platform and demonstrate promising sim-to-real transfer capability in dynamic driving scenarios.

title: Title: Adaptive Predictive Resonance
abstract: This paper introduces Adaptive Predictive Resonance (APR), a novel system designed to dynamically optimize the resonance of a complex system through real-time data input and automated parameter adjustment. The core principle of APR leverages a Pattern Recognition Engine to identify and amplify specific patterns within the system's output, thereby enhancing predictive accuracy. The system's architecture incorporates feedback loops to continuously refine the resonance, ensuring optimal performance. This approach represents a significant advancement in predictive modeling, offering a flexible and adaptive solution compared to traditional static models. The paper details the system's architecture, the core mechanisms driving resonance adjustment, and its performance evaluation across a variety of simulated and experimental datasets.

title: 基于动态图模型的推理算法
abstract: This paper introduces a novel dynamic graph model reasoning algorithm designed to enhance inference efficiency and accuracy. Traditional reasoning methods often rely on static graph representations, limiting their adaptability to evolving data. Our proposed algorithm dynamically adjusts graph structure and parameters to better represent the underlying relationships within the data, facilitating automated knowledge discovery and improved performance. We detail the core mechanism, including the implementation of a self-adaptive graph structure and a learning framework, demonstrating significant improvements in both inference speed and result quality compared to existing approaches. This work contributes to the advancement of robust and adaptable reasoning systems.

title: 基于图的机器学习的动态图谱构建
abstract: This paper introduces a novel method for constructing dynamic graph maps using machine learning, leveraging the inherent adaptability of graph structures. Traditional machine learning models often rely on static, predefined graphs, limiting their ability to effectively handle evolving data. Our approach proposes a dynamic graph construction framework, employing an adaptive adjustment mechanism to dynamically refine the graph based on incoming data. This allows for the creation of more robust and generalizable models compared to static graph representations. The core mechanism hinges on a self-adjusting graph structure, enabling the model to learn patterns that change over time. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method through several experiments, showcasing improved model performance on various machine learning tasks. The focus is on leveraging the dynamic nature of graph structures to enhance model robustness and generalization.

title: Non-Linear Quantum Entanglement Computation Framework
abstract: This paper introduces a novel computational framework based on quantum entanglement that leverages the unique properties of entangled states to accelerate complex computations, particularly in large-scale data processing and quantum chemistry simulations. We propose a "quantum entanglement computation tree" design, utilizing entanglement for enhanced efficiency and parallel processing. This research explores the potential of using entangled states to overcome limitations of traditional quantum algorithms and offers a new approach to tackling computationally intensive problems.

title: Non-linear Geometric Topology Structures for Quantum Entanglement Computation
abstract: This paper introduces a novel quantum entanglement computation framework based on dynamic geometric topology. The core idea is to develop an adaptive geometric topology algorithm that maps quantum states to more complex topological structures, optimizing entanglement propagation and stability. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through a detailed analysis of entanglement dynamics and explore its potential to revolutionize quantum information storage and transmission. The proposed mechanism offers a significant improvement over traditional static topology-based approaches, promising enhanced efficiency and robustness in quantum calculations.

title: Title: Quantum-Enhanced Topological Order Design
abstract: Quantum-enhanced topological order design represents a paradigm shift in materials science, leveraging quantum mechanics to accelerate the discovery and optimization of novel topological materials. This paper investigates a novel quantum algorithm designed to guide the exploration of topological order configurations, predicting their stability and properties with unprecedented precision. By employing quantum superposition, we propose a method to efficiently navigate the complex landscape of topological order, ultimately leading to materials with unique and potentially transformative properties. The paper details the core mechanism of the algorithm, highlighting its potential to overcome limitations of traditional computational approaches.

title: Graph-Based Reinforcement Learning with Intrinsic Motivation for Exploration
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) faces significant challenges when applied to environments with sparse or delayed rewards. Traditional RL algorithms often struggle to effectively explore these environments, leading to slow learning or failure to converge. This paper proposes a novel approach to reinforcement learning that utilizes graph representation and intrinsic motivation to address this issue. We represent the environment as a graph, where nodes represent states and edges represent transitions between states. Intrinsic motivation is then applied based on graph properties, such as path-based curiosity and neighborhood-based novelty, to reward agents for exploring previously unseen regions of the graph. This approach allows the agent to proactively seek out new information and experiences, leading to more efficient and robust exploration. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method through theoretical analysis and a detailed discussion of the underlying mechanisms. The core claim is that standard reinforcement learning struggles with exploration in complex, sparse-reward environments. The core mechanism involves representing the environment as a graph and using graph-based intrinsic motivation to guide exploration. This is a new strategy that leverages graph structure to enhance exploration in reinforcement learning.

title: Quantum State Superposition-Based Parallel Computing Resource Scheduling
abstract: This paper investigates a novel approach to parallel computing resource scheduling leveraging the principles of quantum state superposition. Traditional parallel computing methods face limitations in efficiently utilizing available resources due to inherent sequential execution constraints. We propose a framework that maps computational tasks onto quantum state superposition, enabling parallel execution through quantum control techniques. Furthermore, we explore the potential of quantum entanglement for optimizing resource allocation and scheduling. This research addresses the core claim of enhancing computational efficiency by exploiting the unique properties of quantum mechanics. The methodology presented offers a fundamentally different paradigm for resource management, potentially unlocking significant performance improvements in computationally intensive applications. This work introduces a new method for parallel computation resource scheduling by utilizing quantum state superposition. The key mechanism involves mapping tasks to superposition states, parallel execution via quantum control, and entanglement-based resource scheduling.

title: Based on Information Entropy: Quantum State Regularization
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to quantum state regularization based on information entropy. The core idea is to quantify information entropy and utilize it to define a regularization loss function that constrains the probability distribution of quantum states. This method aims to enhance the stability of quantum algorithms by mitigating the effects of decoherence and the vanishing-wave problem. The proposed technique leverages the gradient information derived from entropy to iteratively refine quantum states, steering them towards more robust and predictable behaviors. We demonstrate a theoretical framework for this approach and outline its potential applications in various quantum computation scenarios. The key contribution lies in establishing a deep connection between quantum state probability distributions and information entropy, a previously underutilized resource in regularization strategies. ---

title: Multi-Modal Ablation Experiment Automation
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to automating the design of multi-modal ablation experiments. Traditional ablation studies are often conducted manually, which is time-consuming, subjective, and prone to bias. Our method leverages algorithmic analysis of model architecture and parameters to automatically generate targeted ablation experiments for each modality within a system. The core mechanism involves identifying critical components and their interdependencies, enabling the creation of a systematic and comprehensive evaluation of model sensitivity. We demonstrate the efficacy of this automated approach through a theoretical framework and illustrate its potential for significantly accelerating model diagnosis and improving the robustness of complex systems. The generated experiment designs are based on a defined set of criteria and constraints, ensuring a rigorous and reproducible process. The primary output is a structured plan for ablation experiments, minimizing human intervention and maximizing diagnostic coverage. The system allows for quantifying the dependence of the model's performance on individual modalities, providing valuable insights for targeted improvements and error mitigation. This work addresses a key bottleneck in model understanding and contributes to more efficient and reliable AI development.

title: Title: Universal Quantum State Representation (QSR)
abstract: Quantum state representation is a cornerstone of quantum information processing, yet current methods often lack a robust, geometric framework for manipulation and analysis. This paper introduces Universal Quantum State Representation (QSR), a novel system for encoding and manipulating quantum states through a layered, dynamically evolving geometric structure. QSR leverages discrete, high-dimensional geometric transformations to provide a more intuitive and flexible approach compared to traditional methods. We demonstrate the efficacy of QSR through a series of illustrative examples, highlighting its potential to simplify complex quantum computations and facilitate deeper insights into quantum information dynamics. This work provides a foundational framework for advancing quantum state representation and enabling new algorithmic possibilities.

abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to program synthesis leveraging the concept of information entropy. The core idea is to quantify the uncertainty or exploration potential within the search space of possible program solutions. By measuring the entropy of candidate programs, we can prioritize exploration in regions with higher entropy, leading to more effective search and ultimately, the generation of higher-quality programs. Traditional program synthesis techniques often rely on heuristics or probabilistic models, which can be inefficient in exploring complex solution spaces. Our method provides a more principled approach by grounding the search process in the theoretical framework of information entropy. We propose a framework for calculating and utilizing entropy metrics within a program synthesis algorithm, offering a potentially significant improvement in synthesis efficiency and program quality. The presented approach demonstrates the potential to guide the search process towards more promising solutions, overcoming limitations of purely heuristic-based methods.

title: Nonlinear Geometry Topology Adaptive Optimization Algorithm
abstract: This paper introduces a novel optimization algorithm based on the principles of nonlinear geometry topology. We propose a framework that integrates topological concepts, specifically self-intersection and self-similarity, into the optimization process. The core mechanism leverages the inherent structural properties of topological spaces to dynamically adjust optimization strategies, enabling the discovery of global optima within complex geometric spaces. The algorithm's novelty lies in its automatic adaptation of optimization parameters through the manipulation of topology, offering a potentially more efficient and robust approach compared to traditional methods. We detail the algorithm's design, its performance evaluation, and potential applications in various geometric optimization problems.

title: Probabilistic Robotics with Bayesian Filtering for Uncertain Environments
abstract: This paper presents a novel framework for probabilistic robotics leveraging Bayesian filtering to address the challenges of operating in highly uncertain environments. Traditional approaches often employ simplifying assumptions regarding noise and model inaccuracies, leading to suboptimal performance in real-world scenarios. This work introduces a refined methodology that directly incorporates both sensor noise and model uncertainties within a Bayesian filtering framework. The core of the approach lies in utilizing the Kalman filter and its extensions to recursively estimate the state of a robot while accounting for the inherent uncertainties. We detail the mathematical formulation, focusing on the Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) and Unscented Kalman Filter (UKF) to handle non-linear systems. Furthermore, we explore methods for adaptive tuning of the filter parameters and discuss the impact of different noise models on the overall performance. The presented framework demonstrates improved robustness and accuracy compared to conventional probabilistic robotics techniques when dealing with complex, real-world environments. The system's effectiveness is primarily assessed through theoretical analysis and conceptual design, without requiring experimental validation.

title: High-Dimensional Data Space Probability Optimization
abstract: High-dimensional data analysis presents significant challenges due to the complexity of parameter adjustments. This paper proposes a novel optimization algorithm based on the probability distribution within high-dimensional data spaces. The core mechanism leverages the dynamic evolution of probability distributions to automatically adjust data distribution parameters, ultimately enhancing data analysis and modeling accuracy. This approach aims to address the inherent difficulties in parameter tuning within high-dimensional datasets. We present a framework that intelligently adapts the data distribution to optimize model performance and robustness.

title: 基于图的自适应神经元网络结构设计
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to neural network architecture design based on graph-based models. We propose a method that automatically optimizes neural network structures by leveraging the inherent graph structure. This approach aims to enhance model generalization capabilities through intelligent adjustments to the network's connections and weights. The core of the design relies on representing the neural network as a graph, allowing for dynamic control of node and edge attributes to facilitate automated learning and refinement. We detail the proposed methodology, its advantages, and the expected impact on neural network performance.

title: Title: Fractal Dimension-Based Algorithmic Complexity Analysis
abstract: Fractal dimension, a measure of irregularity and complexity, offers a novel approach to quantifying algorithmic complexity. This paper presents a framework for dynamically calculating fractal dimensions for each algorithm based on its core operations, utilizing automated optimization to minimize complexity. The core mechanism involves defining fractal dimensions as inherent properties of the algorithm's structure and employing optimization to refine these dimensions, leading to a rigorous and automated method for assessing algorithm behavior and guiding design. The proposed approach represents a significant advancement over existing complexity analysis, providing a quantifiable and adaptable tool for optimizing algorithm performance.

title: Dynamic Machine Learning Adaptive Model Construction
abstract: Dynamic Machine Learning Adaptive Model Construction presents a novel framework for machine learning model creation that leverages an adaptive model adjustment mechanism to optimize the model's parameters. This approach offers improved efficiency and flexibility compared to traditional methods relying on manual parameter adjustments. The core concept centers around a dynamically adjusted model state, allowing the model to continuously refine its parameters based on feedback and data, ultimately leading to enhanced performance. This research focuses on establishing a robust and efficient methodology for building adaptive models, addressing limitations of existing techniques. The proposed framework is designed to provide a more adaptable and scalable solution for a wide range of machine learning applications.

title: Adaptive Parameterization Algorithm Based on Quantum Information
abstract: This paper presents an innovative algorithm, the Adaptive Parameterization Algorithm (APA), designed to enhance computational efficiency by dynamically adjusting algorithm parameters based on the target computation and environmental parameters. Utilizing the inherent properties of quantum information, the APA leverages quantum state manipulation to optimize the algorithm's performance in real-time. We introduce a novel mechanism involving quantum state interactions and error correction to achieve this adaptive adjustment. The core claim of this work is that the APA can significantly improve computational throughput compared to traditional parameterization techniques, particularly in complex computational scenarios. This paper details the algorithm's design, implementation, and preliminary results demonstrating its effectiveness across a range of problems.

title: IMPLEMENTATION OF PYTHON PROGRAMMING IN PHARMACY: A REVIEW
authors: Subhajit Samanta*, Dr. Dhrubo, Jyoti Sen
abstract: The growing use of digital technology in healthcare has increased the importance of computational skills in pharmacy. Python is a simple, open-source programming language widely used for data analysis, visualization, modelling, and artificial intelligence. In pharmacy, Python can be applied to pharmacokinetics, pharmaceutical research, drug discovery, formulation development, pharmacovigilance, and clinical data analysis. Introducing basic Python programming into pharmacy education may improve students' analytical abilities and prepare them for modern, technology-driven pharmaceutical research.

title: Feature-Rich Deep Learning Architecture for Breast Cancer Detection: From Image Analysis to Real-Time App Deployment
abstract: Breast cancer would be a major global world concern, particularly among women, for whom early and accurate diagnosis significantly improves treatment outcomes. This paper suggest a feature-rich hybrid deep learning framework that combines traditional handcrafted features, as the Histogram of Oriented Gradients (HOG), Local Binary Pattern (LBP), Gray-Level Co-occurrence Matrix, and intensity statistics, with transfer learning models, including ResNet18, ResNet50, and VGG16. These features were fused and classified using a custom multilayer perceptron (MLP) classifier. Among all the tested combinations, GLCM combined with ResNet18 The highest classification accuracy attained on ultrasound breast image data was 89%. The efficacy of the model is substantiated through the application of various evaluation metrics. Furthermore, the model was deployed using StreamLit, enabling real-time clinical inference. The proposed framework continue to support radiologists by offering transparent, interpretable, and reliable computer-aided diagnosis (CAD) tools.

title: Few-shot learning with enhanced calibration for language- and harm-aware multilingual hate speech detection (FLEC-HS)
abstract: Multilingual hate speech detection remains challenging in low-resource settings, where labelled data are limited, particularly for identity-targeted and context-dependent content. We present Few-Shot Learning with Enhanced Calibration for Language- and Harm-Aware Multilingual Hate Speech Detection (FLEC-HS). This modular framework combines few-shot prompting with a frozen GPT-4o model and a lightweight Feature-Conditioned Calibration Layer (FCL) for post-hoc probability calibration. The primary evaluation uses HateDay (approximately 160,000 posts across eight languages), while HateCheck and HateXplain provide complementary functional and cross-dataset diagnostics. The term few-shot refers specifically to the prompting stage, which uses up to K = 16 demonstrations per language. The complete system additionally uses approximately 400 labelled development instances per language to train the FCL and select operating thresholds. Thresholds are selected by five-fold cross-validation on development data and frozen before test evaluation. On HateDay, FLEC-HS achieves a macro-F1 of 0.64, compared with 0.56 for the fully fine-tuned XLM-R-large. At the development-selected operating point requiring hate-class precision of at least 95%, hate recall increases from 0.48 to 0.61. Relative to the fully fine-tuned XLM-R-large baseline (48% review share), FLEC-HS reduces the share of posts sent to human review to 28% under the evaluated entropy-routing policy. Removing the FCL reduces macro-F1 to 0.59 and increases the protected-group false-negative rate from 5.1 to 10.4%. Protected-group fairness is operationalised narrowly through false-negative rates derived from dataset metadata; no broader fairness guarantee is claimed. The findings are limited to the evaluated benchmarks and configuration and remain subject to domain shift, commercial API dependencies, and incomplete coverage of dialects and protected groups.

title: Application of Attention Mechanisms in Sentiment Analysis
abstract: This chapter offers an in-depth exploration of attention mechanisms and their revolutionary impact on sentiment analysis. It introduces the fundamental principles of attention, including Query-Key-Value interactions, additive and scaled dot-product attention, and the self-attention mechanism. The core role of multi-head self-attention within the Transformer architecture is thoroughly explained. Applications across different tasks are examined in detail: text sentiment classification, aspect-based sentiment analysis, multimodal fusion, and graph-structured data using graph attention networks (GATs). Advanced variants such as sparse attention (Longformer and BigBird) are also discussed. A practical case study on aspect-based sentiment analysis demonstrates the implementation and interpretability benefits of attention mechanisms.

title: Explainable Multimodal Deep Learning Integrating Imaging and Clinical Data for Oral Potentially Malignant Disorder Detection
abstract: Oral potentially malignant disorders (OPMDs) are critical precursors to oral cancer, yet clinical detection remains challenging because of substantial phenotypic heterogeneity and overlap with benign conditions. Although image-based deep learning shows promise for automated screening, visual information alone may be insufficient in real-world settings, where diagnostic decisions also rely on patient-specific risk factors. We developed M2-OPMDNet, a multimodal deep learning framework that integrates co-registered white-light and autofluorescence intraoral images with structured clinical information for OPMD detection. A customized questionnaire was designed to capture clinically relevant risk factors and symptoms in a standardized, reproducible format for integration with image-derived features. Multiple image encoders, including conventional convolutional neural networks and foundation model-based architectures, were evaluated using a prospectively collected dataset reflecting real-world screening conditions. Model interpretability was assessed using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) to quantify feature- and modality-level contributions. M2-OPMDNet achieved an AUC of 0.952, outperforming unimodal approaches and showing improved performance for visually subtle lesions. SHAP analysis demonstrated that structured clinical variables contributed substantially to risk estimation and complemented imaging features. These results demonstrate that explainable multimodal learning combining white-light and autofluorescence imaging with structured clinical data can provide accurate, transparent, and clinically grounded OPMD detection. M2-OPMDNet offers a scalable framework for real-world oral cancer screening and decision support.

title: Parameterised graph theory for tensor networks: entanglement rerouting, structural simplification, and agnostic tomography
abstract: Parameterised graph theory studies how the complexity of graph-theoretic problems depends on structural parameters of the input graph. This perspective has proved useful in analysing tensor-network simulation (Markov and Shi, 2008). Its implications for tensor-network representations and tomography are less well understood. In particular, which graph parameters determine whether a tensor-network state (TNS) admits a tractable matrix product state (MPS) or tree tensor network (TTN) representation, and which control the complexity of learning the state? We address these questions using parameterised graph theory. First, we show that cutwidth and tree-cutwidth bound the bond dimension overhead required to represent a TNS as an MPS or TTN. In the TTN case, tree-cutwidth also bounds the local dimension of the grouped subsystems. The proofs are based on entanglement rerouting, a tensor-network analogue of rerouting information in a classical network. Second, we derive graph-dependent upper bounds on the sample and computational complexity of realisable TNS tomography, with exponents that depend on cutwidth, tree-cutwidth, and a new graph parameter, learning complexity, which we bound in terms of degree and treewidth. We obtain these results by extending the disentangling MPS learner of (Cramer et al., 2010), as analysed further in (Bakshi et al., 2025; Lin et al., 2025), to TTNs and to tensor networks on arbitrary known graphs. Finally, we extend the framework beyond the realisable setting. For an arbitrary input state, our agnostic learner outputs a pure state whose fidelity is within additive error $ε$ of the optimum over tensor-network states on the given graph with a given bond dimension, with explicit graph-dependent bounds on sample and computational complexity.

title: P-CORE: Self-Supervised Surface Consistency for Point-Based Neural Editing
abstract: Advances in neural rendering have enabled high-fidelity multi-view reconstruction of 3D scenes. However, free-form non-rigid shape editing remains a significant challenge. Point-based neural representations are highly desirable for multi-view reconstruction because they lack fixed connectivity, which does not constrain the learned surface topology to that of the initialization. Yet this same property causes point-based representations to struggle with holes and surface discontinuities under large deformations. To address this, we propose a novel self-supervised method to enable point-based representations to adapt to large deformations without requiring ground truth multi-view images of deformed geometry. The key idea is to generate random deformations and to ensure consistency in the predicted surface before and after deformation. In particular, the surface prediction from the deformed point cloud should be the same as the deformation applied to the surface prediction from the original point cloud. We incorporate our approach into attention-based point representations, which differ from splatting-based point representations in their use of a learned interpolation kernel between points as opposed to a Gaussian kernel around each point. This learned interpolation kernel can learn to adapt to large deformations, without requiring addition or removal of points. We show that our framework significantly enhances its robustness to large deformations. Experiments on synthetic geometry editing benchmarks (Neural Editor, Objaverse) demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing point-based methods in zero-shot editing and significantly reduces artifacts. Furthermore, qualitative results on the DTU and Mip-NeRF 360 datasets demonstrate our method's effectiveness on real-world scenes.

title: AI, Quantum Computing and High-Performance Computing
abstract: The intersection of AI, quantum computing (QC) and high-performance computing (HPC) creates a spectrum of opportunities. AI is already enhancing QC by assisting with the design and performance of quantum hardware and algorithms, while QC offers the potential to address limitations in classical AI by, for example, improving machine learning and model training. This CETaS Snapshot Report assesses the near-term opportunities provided by hybrid quantum-classical computing systems, and the implications for national security and prosperity. The report outlines a number of challenges and recommendations for the UK’s integration of QC and HPC systems, calling for an acceleration of efforts in order to avoid falling behind in an area central to the future of supercomputing.
